sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, why can't ML teams just commit our CSV and Parquet files directly into standard Git repositories? Git is already the gold standard for software version control!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Because Git stores a full compressed copy of every modified binary file in the dot-git packfile! When you edit a 10-gigabyte feature matrix, your repository clone size doubles. After a dozen sprints, developers face 100-gigabyte clones and out-of-memory crashes!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: And standard line-by-line diffs like git diff are totally useless on dense binary floating-point tensors and compressed parquet blocks!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Exactly! That is why we decouple the lightweight Control Plane in Git from the immutable Data Plane in Content-Addressable Object Storage, using Merkle trees to guarantee end-to-end cryptographic integrity.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Wait, Dr. Nova! If the 12-gigabyte feature parquet file is stored in S3, does my workstation download the entire 12 gigabytes every time I checkout a new Git branch?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Never! Your workspace uses reflinks or hardlinks pointing into the local cache. When you switch branches, Git only updates a tiny 150-byte text pointer file. If the underlying data did not change, zero bytes are transferred or duplicated on disk!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: So Git stays blazing fast, while DVC or Git-LFS handles fetching only the mutated blobs from S3 when explicitly requested with dvc pull!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Why do we call it Content-Addressable Storage? What makes an address based on content so much better than traditional filesystem paths like slash data slash train dot csv?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Because file paths are mutable labels! A developer can overwrite train dot csv in place, silently corrupting your training data while keeping the exact same filename. In CAS, the address is the hash of the raw bytes. If you change a single byte, the address changes completely!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: And if two engineers have the same 5-gigabyte embeddings file under different names, CAS immediately detects they have the same hash and stores only one copy!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: So if our dataset contains ten thousand image files, and one single pixel changes in image nine thousand, what happens to the Merkle tree?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: The hash of that single image changes. Because that image is an entry in its parent directory, the directory hash changes. And because the directory hash changes, the root tree hash and the commit hash change completely!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: And all the other nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine images retain their exact same SHA-256 hashes, so we only store one new blob while the rest are deduplicated!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Wait—you mean an edge vehicle with limited LTE cellular bandwidth can verify that a new 10-megabyte LiDAR frame belongs to a 10-terabyte training corpus by downloading only 640 bytes?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Exactly! In a balanced Merkle tree of 1,048,576 frames, depth d is log 2 of 2 to the 20th, which is exactly 20. The edge client hashes its frame, hashes it with 20 sibling hashes up the tree, and checks if the result matches the published 32-byte root hash!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: That eliminates 99.9999 percent of data transfer! Tampering with a single byte in the frame breaks the root match immediately!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Below us in Lab 1, the golden commit node at the top connects through the teal Merkle directory tree down to three large binary blobs!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Click Mutate Labels v1.1.0 below: notice how labels dot csv turns coral with a new hash, causing the tree and commit root to update while features and embeddings remain untouched in white! Then click Tamper 1 Byte to watch the red integrity alert fire!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 1 tests SA 8.5.1! Watch carefully: only part 1 has a modified float in row 4,912, while part 0 and part 2 are totally untouched! Select the correct diagnosis in the quiz below me!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the formula: 1 minus 1 over K times 1 minus delta! That means the more releases you make, the closer your savings get to 1 minus delta!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Precisely! With naive snapshots, twenty releases of a 100-gigabyte dataset consumes two terabytes. With CAS at 5 percent churn, it takes only 195 gigabytes. That is over 90 percent savings on physical storage and cloud transfer bills!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: And because unchanged chunks share the exact same hash address, multiple pipelines can train on different historical snapshots without duplicating data!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: If a team renames a column like SystolicBP to systolic_blood_pressure_mmhg, why can't that just be a Minor bump? It's just a name change!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Think of downstream inference! Any automated production model expecting df bracket SystolicBP will immediately throw a KeyError and crash the entire pipeline! Any breaking change that invalidates existing consumer code requires a Major bump from v2 dot 4 dot 1 straight to v3 dot 0 dot 0!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Whereas appending ten thousand new patient rows with the exact same columns is a backwards-compatible Minor bump to v2 dot 5 dot 0!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the scaling curves in Lab 2 below! The red line shows naive copying rocketing upward to 500 gigabytes after 10 releases of a 50-gigabyte dataset!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Now look at the teal CAS curve: with 10 percent churn, storage is only 95 gigabytes, capturing 81 percent savings! Slide the releases slider up to 25 and watch savings approach the 90 percent asymptotic ceiling!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Time for Checkpoint 2! N equals 2 to the 20th frames, and each SHA-256 sibling hash is 32 bytes! Compute depth d and transferred bandwidth in the quiz below me!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, both case studies prove that large models cannot survive without Content-Addressable Storage! If BigScience had cloned full snapshots for every evaluation run, trans-European network lines would have choked completely!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Yes! Hashing tokenized chunks into 50-gigabyte immutable blocks meant distributed compute nodes downloaded each shard exactly once. Unchanged data was shared seamlessly across training and evaluation runs!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Final Checkpoint! Compute 120 times 1 plus 14 times 0.08, and remember what happens to a downstream model when a column is renamed or deleted! Select the right answer below me!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: So if we are working with tabular data in Spark or Trino, we use Delta Lake time-travel. But for raw images, audio, and multimodal datasets, we use DVC or Git-LFS with Content-Addressable remotes!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Exactly! Choose the tool matched to your payload: ACID table logs for tabular data warehouses, and Content-Addressable Merkle DAGs for unstructured binary corpora!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the CASStorageEngine implementation: the blob_pool dictionary indexes solely by digest! When Version 1.1.0 commits with unchanged features and embeddings, the dictionary keys already exist, so zero extra memory is allocated!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: And look at the verified assertions on the right: naive storage records 6.6 megabytes across the two versions, while CAS stores only 3.6 megabytes—capturing 45 percent deduplication savings on the very first release!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: What a masterclass! We transformed data version control from messy, crashing Git repositories into a clean decoupled architecture with Merkle trees, logarithmic audit paths, deduplication scaling, and SemVer contracts!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Spot on, Kaito! Now that we have mastered the mathematical foundations, Lesson 8.6 puts them into practice with hands-on DVC commands, multi-cloud remotes, and automated reproducible pipelines!
